Text | Fanyu Meng, Er Mu

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Introduction

I recently came across a collaboration between Alibaba’s Genie acoustics team, the people behind the Tmall Genie smart speaker, and Boston Acoustics, which they described as an attempt to integrate sound tuning within a “smart acoustics” technical framework. As far as I know, this is the first time a Chinese manufacturer has put forward such a concept and laid out a complete system behind it. “Smart acoustics” is not, in fact, the established name of any recognized branch of acoustics. It may be easier to understand if we split it into “smart” and “acoustics.” The smart home (home automation) is the idea of bringing intelligent information technology into domestic life to improve its quality. The smart home market was worth nearly US$65 billion in 2020 and is expected to reach US$163 billion by 2028. Sound is a major channel for exchanging information, and acoustics, from voice interaction and speech recognition to all kinds of audio technology that improve the listening experience, plays an ever larger role in the smart home. So, to put it roughly, smart acoustics is the umbrella term for the acoustic technologies involved in the smart home. Today, let’s talk about how smart acoustics developed and the acoustic technologies it involves.

How smart acoustics developed

The most important acoustic device in the smart home is probably the smart speaker. In 2022 the smart speaker market was worth US$6.6 billion, more than 10% of the whole smart home market. In the age of smart devices, a speaker no longer just plays songs: it is an intelligent device that combines multiple sensors, AI, speech and acoustic algorithms and a host of other cutting-edge technologies.

The smart speaker arguably began with the launch of the Amazon Echo in 2014. Alexa, the AI at its core, could understand users’ commands and play songs. From then on, smart speakers burst onto the scene, quickly took over the market and gradually became the hub of the smart home. Beyond playing music, they spread into other parts of home life: you can ask about the weather, the stock market, travel plans or store opening hours, shop online or chat about other general topics. Smart speakers can also control lighting and air conditioning, set timers and alarms, and much more. They have found their way into every corner of domestic life.

Besides Amazon with the Echo, the more successful makers abroad include Google, Sonos, Apple and Harman, while in China the main players are Baidu, Xiaomi, Huawei and Alibaba. With so many contenders vying for the crown, what secret martial arts does each clan leader have up their sleeve? Let’s look at the main acoustic technologies involved…

The technologies of smart acoustics

The whole process of a smart acoustic interaction starts at a person’s mouth and ends at a person’s ear. The user gives a command; with the help of sound source localization and noise suppression, the smart speaker’s microphone array hears it clearly. The speaker’s processor then runs a series of processing steps to perform various kinds of recognition and tuning, and the reply or the music is delivered through the loudspeaker to the listener’s ear.

1. Voiceprint recognition

Voiceprint recognition is also called speaker recognition or voice biometric recognition; in English, “speaker recognition” is the more widely used term. As the name suggests, its job is to identify who is speaking by analyzing their voice. Voiceprint recognition is a form of biometric identification. There are many biometric technologies, which fall broadly into two groups: those based on physical traits and those based on behavioral traits. The first group includes face, fingerprint, retina and iris recognition; the second includes voiceprint, gesture and signature recognition. The table below compares how each technology performs in terms of accuracy, ease of use, user acceptance, ease of deployment and cost:

The table makes it clear that voiceprint recognition performs very well overall, and studies have shown that it can also match iris, fingerprint and face recognition for security. Everyone’s voice is unique, and that uniqueness comes from our individually unique vocal anatomy. If you’d like to know more about how the voice is produced, see our earlier article How do we produce our voices? Compared with the other technologies, voiceprint recognition works at a distance, which makes it better suited to smart speaker systems.

A short story:

The development of voiceprint recognition can be traced back to 1932 and the famous US Federal Kidnapping Act, often called the “Lindbergh Law.” That year, the 20-month-old son of the American aviator Charles Lindbergh was kidnapped and, tragically, killed. When Charles handed over the ransom, he was sitting in a car and never saw the kidnapper’s face, but he did hear his voice. More than two years later a suspect was arrested; Charles listened to the man’s voice and testified at the trial that it was exactly the voice he had heard two years before. The case drew enormous attention across the United States, and it inspired the researcher Frances McGehee to begin the earliest research into identifying people by their voices. The main milestones since then are as follows:

Key milestones in the development of voiceprint recognition

Block diagram of a voiceprint recognition system

The block diagram above shows how a voiceprint recognition system is put together. Voiceprint recognition is a kind of pattern recognition with two main phases, training and testing, and its core steps are preprocessing, feature extraction and modeling.

2. Speech recognition

Voiceprint recognition tells the speaker who is talking to it; what teaches it to understand what is being said is speech recognition. Below we introduce two common traditional approaches: the acoustic-phonetic approach and the pattern recognition approach.

The acoustic-phonetic approach was proposed by Hemdal and Hughes in 1967. It holds that speech is made up of basic linguistic units (phonemes), each of which can be characterized by a set of physical acoustic parameters. These parameters are functions of the speaker and of the neighboring units, and those functional relationships are easy for a machine to learn. The first step is spectral analysis of the speech signal, followed by extraction of acoustic parameter features, and then segmentation and labeling: the utterance is cut into many shorter, independent segments, and each one is given a phonetic label and matched to specific words. This approach never came into wide use.

The second is the pattern recognition (pattern matching) approach, which has four steps: feature analysis, pattern training, pattern classification and logical decision. Before training, the input speech signal has to be preprocessed, which is the feature analysis step. Pattern training creates reference patterns, either with templates or with a statistical model (the hidden Markov model). During classification, an unknown pattern is compared against the reference patterns and the differences are computed. For a long time, this approach attracted a great deal of attention and development.

3. Sound source localization

Sound source localization lets the speaker hear where a person is speaking from, so that it can focus on that direction and capture the command with a relatively high signal-to-noise ratio. The most common technique is beamforming, which uses a microphone array to locate the source. Beamforming may date back as far as the First World War. I gave a brief introduction to it in an earlier article in my series on sound visualization, A history of acoustics: sound visualization, part 2.

A Perrin acoustic array in use during the First World War to detect the bearing of enemy aircraft. Its inventor, Sergeant Jean Perrin (far right), won the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Take the simplest method, delay-and-sum beamforming, as an example. We place two phones on a plane with a grid drawn on it. Each phone has a loudspeaker that emits a sound signal, which is picked up by a set of microphones on another plane. In panel b, the vertical axis is the microphones and the horizontal axis is time. You can see that the signal arrives at each microphone with a different delay. That makes sense: each microphone is a different distance from the loudspeaker, and the distance divided by the speed of sound gives the delay. Now look at panel d. We scan the grid cell by cell, row by row, treating each cell as a candidate source position. For each cell we compute its distance to every microphone, and from that the delay, and then compensate for the delay along the time axis. Because the cell in panel d is not where the real source is, the color plot below it still shows delays after compensation. In panel e we have clearly found the right position: once the delays are compensated, the signals from all the microphones line up exactly. At that point, summing all the microphone signals gives the largest value, so by searching for the spatial maximum in this way we can find the loudspeaker’s true position [4].

Of course, if things were really this simple, those of us in R&D would starve. So however surreal reality gets, we should be grateful for it ;) Closely spaced sources, low-frequency sources, room reverberation and high background noise, for example, all make accurate localization by beamforming harder. Optimization methods such as MVDR and deconvolution methods such as DAMAS and CLEAN can improve localization accuracy to some extent. Some sources also report that the FRIDA (finite rate of innovation sampling based algorithm) and MUSIC (MUsical Signal Classification) algorithms are the most robust, followed by SRP-PHAT (steered-response power phase transform) and TOPS (test of orthogonality of projected subspaces), and then by WAVES (weighted average of signal subspaces) and CSSM (coherent signal subspace method). For angular resolution, FRIDA again does well, followed by MUSIC and SRP-PHAT, and correlation-based methods do worse than non-correlation-based ones. In recent years, beamforming based on machine learning and deep learning has emerged and brought big gains in localization accuracy and robustness; we will come to that below.

4. Echo cancellation

Echo cancellation is an important technology in telecommunications and is widely used in mobile phones, teleconferencing systems, hearing aids and more. So what is an echo? How does it arise, what harm does it do and why do we need to cancel it? Some of you have probably had this happen: you are on the phone with a friend, you finish a sentence, and immediately you hear that same sentence come back through the earpiece, repeated several times and loud, so that you can barely make out what your friend is saying. That delayed copy of your own voice is an echo. It serves no purpose, it should not be there, and it badly degrades the quality and experience of the call.

In the figure above, w is the far-end talker’s speech signal, x is the impulse response of the echo path, w*x is the echo signal, s is the near-end talker’s speech, d is the signal picked up by the near-end microphone and e is the error. The far-end talker’s voice is played through the near-end loudspeaker, picked up by the near-end microphone either directly or via reflections, and sent back to the far end. That, in essence, is how an echo arises.

So how do we cancel it? As the figure suggests, we estimate the impulse response w of the echo path and convolve it with the far-end signal to obtain an estimate of the echo. Subtracting that estimate from the microphone signal before transmitting or playing it solves the problem. And how do we estimate the impulse response of the echo path? With an adaptive filter. Common algorithms include LMS, NLMS, RLS and APA.

Compared with telephone calls, adaptive echo cancellation matters even more in the far-field use case of a smart speaker. Why? Imagine the speaker is blasting a song we love, and we suddenly want it to tell us today’s weather. Normally we are much farther from the speaker’s microphones than its own loudspeaker is, and our voice is not as loud as the playback. Our command to play the weather is completely buried in the music the speaker is playing, so the speaker never hears it. Echo cancellation is therefore essential; without it, the speaker cannot even tell whether we have given it a command, let alone interact with us. Put simply, echo cancellation is what lets the speaker hear what we say.

5. Dereverberation

Once echo cancellation has dealt with the effect of the speaker’s own playback on our voice commands, the reverberation of the room still gets in the way. What is room reverberation? Part of the sound from a source reaches our ears directly, while another part arrives only after being reflected or scattered by the walls, furniture and other objects in the room. These late-arriving sounds are called reverberant sound. The longer the delay, the stronger the reverberant effect. When it is too strong, with a delay of 50 ms for example, the ear can already tell the direct sound and the reflection apart, which spoils what we hear: it becomes hard to follow what people are saying, or the music sounds poor. A moderate amount, with delays of 10–30 ms for example, actually enhances our listening experience, thanks to the temporal masking of the ear. But a smart speaker’s ears, its microphones, have no such temporal masking. Of the voice command we speak, the delayed part caused by reverberation, as opposed to the part that reaches the microphones directly, is very harmful to the speech recognition that follows; in other words, it stops the speaker from hearing us clearly. It must be dealt with, and the techniques for doing so are called speech dereverberation. There are three main families of dereverberation algorithms. The first is beamforming, a spatial filtering approach that lets the speaker hear only sound from a particular direction and cancels or attenuates sound from all others. The second is speech enhancement, which can be further divided into methods based on statistical models, methods based on LPC (linear predictive coding) and methods based on eigenvalue decomposition. The third is blind deconvolution.

The video below shows someone speaking in a room with very particular reverberation, known as a reverberation chamber. Can’t you almost see the sound bouncing around all over the place? Maddening, isn’t it? Can you make out what the person in the video is saying?

6. Bringing in AI

AI has probably become a worn-out, “has-been” buzzword. Unlike many other hyped technologies, though, AI has genuinely been deployed in industry for years, solving very real problems in every field, even if academia latched onto it long ago and turned it into a frenzied rat race: these days, if your paper doesn’t mention AI, you can barely show your face.

AI stands for artificial intelligence. It already shows up in every one of the technologies above, and the key for the future is to integrate acoustics and AI well. In sound source localization, for example, if the background noise is very loud or many people are talking at once, traditional beamforming and its improved variants are limited both in how precisely they can locate the person giving the command and in computational efficiency. A convolutional neural network can now solve this problem. Put simply, the beam pattern at each frequency is fed into the network as input, the pattern of the true source serves as the reference, and the network learns to remove the spurious spots from the beam pattern [5].

The same principle applies to speech recognition and voiceprint recognition. For instance, the spectrograms of different commands spoken by different people can serve as the network’s input, and by continually collecting data to grow the database, recognition accuracy goes up. This is in fact much like AI for image processing: a beam pattern and a spectrogram are, at heart, both images [6].

To improve a model’s computational efficiency and accuracy, we often need to extract more useful features so that the input parameters are more orthogonal, in other words, more representative. Besides working on the audio signal itself, we can also bring in other sensors, such as tactile sensors, EEG (electroencephalography), EMG (electromyography), cameras and IMUs (inertial measurement units), and fuse the signals from multiple sensors (multimodal fusion). That lets the network recognize the user’s intent more accurately, understand what they need and improve their experience.

7. EQ, tuning and golden ears

When sound is played back through a loudspeaker, the speaker itself and the playback environment usually prevent us from reproducing the original signal faithfully. This is down to the physical limitations of the speaker and to reflections of the sound in the room. An equalizer, or EQ for short, does what its name says: it equalizes the sound, compensating for the effects of the speaker and the room mentioned above. Ideally, whatever signal we put in, we should hear exactly the same signal come out. To take a simple and not entirely accurate example: if the sound is played at an intensity of 1 at every frequency, then what I hear should also be 1 everywhere, and the job of the EQ is to bring everything that isn’t 1 back to 1. We can add suitable filters wherever the response is not 1, boosting where it falls below 1 and cutting where it rises above. In reality, of course, we aim higher. If we want a fuller, deeper sound, we might raise the low frequencies to 1.5; if we want a brighter sound, we can raise the high frequencies to 1.5; or if female voices are particularly loud around 600 Hz, we add a notch filter there to take some energy out. One level up is spatial audio: with a set of speakers, if we want the listener to feel that “the stage is in front of them,” then besides tuning we also have to account for the different delays from each speaker to the ear.

Overtuning, however, can strip music of the emotion it is meant to convey, much as too thick a patina can bury an antique. That is why some smart speakers now promote the idea of a “no-patina” equalizer.

Tuning curves [7]

It is unrealistic to claim that cold curves alone can deliver a perfect listening experience. Our ears are extremely picky, so a curve can look beautiful and still sound unpleasant. Or say I want a deep, full sound: should the low end go up to 1.5 or to 1.49? This is where “golden ears” come in. The “million-dollar sound tuners” that come up so often on Zhihu are exactly that group of people with golden ears. Writing this reminds me of an all-powerful client on a project at my previous company. They had a few golden-eared experts, and the units these experts judged by ear to be good or defective became the training samples for our machine learning. Because the experts’ hearing sensitivity was not linear and time-invariant, our models often performed poorly -_-.

I’m an expert. Aren’t I cute?

That is one job I will never be able to do. Longtime readers may remember that I once posted my own audiogram… Honestly, I think I could do with an EQ inside my ears… If the topic interests you, take a look at A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 2.

Somebody’s audiogram

Where smart acoustics is heading

Smart acoustics is built on the smart speaker, so we naturally cannot ignore what a speaker is fundamentally for: playing music. As the technology develops, we must keep a close eye on people’s listening experience. Here, briefly, are some of the future directions for smart speaker audio that come to mind.

3D audio

This is not a technology exclusive to smart speakers but one that applies to speakers in general. Once there is at least one smart speaker in the home, we can start thinking about 3D audio. Sitting on the sofa listening to a Jay Chou concert, say (Jay Chou being the Mandopop superstar), we can feel as if we are really there. To take the simplest example of 3D audio: we are on the sofa, and Jay is singing on the stage right in front of us. When he walks over to the left of the stage to interact with the audience, what we hear should match what we see; even with our eyes closed, we would know he had moved to the left of the stage. An earlier article described in detail the technologies Facebook Reality Labs has been developing for 3D audio: Hearing the future: audio in the future life

Dr. Li, one of our group of authors, worked with the lead of the 3D audio effort while doing research at Facebook Reality Labs.

Multiroom audio

This one is easy to grasp. We are listening to music on a smart speaker in the living room and want to go and spend some time in the bedroom. The obvious thing to do is carry the speaker into the bedroom. But here is the catch: with several smart speakers, that becomes rather impractical. So the next evolution of 3D audio is multiroom 3D audio: smart speakers in every room, sensors tracking where the listener is, and 3D audio rendered in real time so the listening experience is never interrupted. Say I lie down and listen to music for a while, then get up to cook: the music follows me all the way to the kitchen and keeps playing while I cook. And it is not only about listening. With this setup you can call on the voice assistant anywhere, at any time, without craning your neck and shouting into the next room.

Personal sound zones

Two people on the same sofa, one listening to a concert and the other to an MIT open lecture, with neither hearing the other’s audio. Pretty cool, right? Beyond indoor spaces, this technology is also a hot research topic for car cabins. It still has many limitations: controlling multiple zones is hard in a reverberant space, for example, and performance varies across frequency ranges, with low frequencies working better than high ones, because high frequencies require a very large number of loudspeakers [Cecchi 2018]. MEMS loudspeakers could solve this problem, since they are small and cheap. MEMS speakers are among the more cutting-edge technologies in acoustics and one of the directions smart speakers could develop in. Dr. Xiaoyu Niu, one of our group of authors, works in the UT Acoustic MEMS Lab at the University of Texas, which has long been researching this area. If you’re interested, have a look at his article on directional MEMS microphones, The most advanced microphone on Earth turns out to be a fly’s ear…

Nonlinear equalization

When we tune with EQ, we are correcting not only the distortion caused by room reflections but also the linear and nonlinear distortion introduced by the loudspeaker and the amplification chain. What we usually call equalization or tuning mainly addresses linear distortion. In recent years, some research has used Volterra filters to model the amplifier–driver–enclosure system and then play the signal out, equalizing both the linear and nonlinear behavior of the system.

Personalized tuning

Tuning tailored to the musical styles a user likes: the system learns the user’s preferences from the frequency content of the music they listen to, creates an equalization curve unique to that user and applies it to the music they play.

Directional sound

True wireless (TWS) earbuds are great, but even the most comfortable earbuds become uncomfortable if you wear them long enough. That is why companies in China and abroad have started developing directional sound technology. A good Israeli friend who shared an office with me during my PhD was working on exactly this a few years ago; they also call the technology “virtual headphones.” In China, as far as I know, the Institute of Acoustics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences is working on it too.

The idea is to combine headphones, loudspeakers and 3D playback into one, keeping the best of each and discarding the rest. It rests on three main principles:

1. A 3D sensor identifies the position of the head, and in particular of the two ears;

2. Highly directional sound is beamed at the ears. Once the positions of the ears are known, the binaural audio signals are modulated onto ultrasound so that each ear can be targeted precisely, and then some nonlinear, self-demodulating method (I don’t know what exactly; if you do, please enlighten me) recovers the original audio at the ears;

3. The ultrasound is emitted by a special loudspeaker, a multi-cell speaker module.

Audio is modulated onto ultrasound and demodulated before it reaches the ear [8]

You wear nothing and still get the effect of headphones. And it can do something loudspeakers cannot: virtual headphones can make a sound audible only to the intended listener and to nobody else. In public spaces that could mean a great deal. Different areas of the same museum room could play different audio for different themes without interfering with each other; a family of three in a car could each listen to their own music without headphones; and people could take phone calls in the office.

Private sound spaces

The concept is very appealing, though I don’t know how well it works in practice. I’m curious how they solve several problems: how accurately the ears can be tracked; whether ultrasound can deliver sound right to the entrance of the ear canal; how errors in the delivery position and in tracking make the HRTFs inaccurate and degrade binaural perception; and how to keep the demodulated sound from spreading into the surrounding space.

According to reports in Chinese AI media such as QbitAI and Leiphone, Alibaba’s Genie acoustics lab has identified four major trends for the future of smart acoustics:

What is most interesting in this overall assessment is the part on music genres and acoustic architecture, where the team seems to be pursuing some consumer-facing technical explorations of its own. Their future products and technology are worth watching. At the level of underlying technology, the adaptive environment-sensing and sound-producing units they propose look like a promising direction.

Recommended reading

Convention says an article like this should end with a summary, but I don’t think that’s really necessary. I’ll leave the ending open and let readers’ imaginations roam (mostly because I don’t think I’m up to writing a comprehensive summary).
